newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU fears EMU woes may gatecrash Amsterdam summit.
newsitem.headline: EU fears EMU woes may gatecrash Amsterdam summit.

text.p: Europe's turbulent ride towards economic and monetary union (EMU) is threatening to spill over into a European Union summit in Amsterdam in two weeks.

The summit was supposed to be largely EMU-free, focusing on the nitty-gritty of internal EU reforms in a new treaty to prepare the 15-member bloc for recruiting members from post-communist eastern Europe.

But the furore over German plans to revalue gold assets in a desperate bid to qualify for EMU, and the election in France of a Socialist government which has promised to review European policy, have raised serious doubts over the prospects for a credible single currency.

As the Union moves into a crucial phase on both EMU and the treaty, financial markets believe the French and German problems in qualifying for EMU give the bloc a stark choice -- launch a weak euro on time or delay the project.
Either way, the credibility of the bloc and its new currency could be severely dented.

The agenda for the June 16-17 summit, dominated by esoteric issues such as subsidiarity, flexibility and transparency, does require agreement on the legal framework of monetary union's Stability Pact. This was agreed at last December's Dublin summit.
French premier Lionel Jospin, who campaigned by opposing an austerity programme launched to help France to meet EMU criteria, has said he would re-open the debate on the pact.
But analysts wonder how committed Paris is to rewriting the deal.

EU diplomats say that politically it is difficult to see how the bloc would reopen talks on the pact, which sets stiff fines for governments participating in EMU if they run excessive budget deficits. Debate is more likely to focus on French concerns about unemployment, they said.

Diplomats remain adamant that summit leaders will not allow EMU to derail efforts to sign the new treaty, the product of an inter-governmental conference (IGC). "Everybody wants to get this out of the way," one said.
"Certainly EMU will be overhanging the summit, but they're very determined to get through the IGC...They've got a lot to do, more than they had to do at Maastricht."
The 1992 Maastricht summit produced the treaty laying down rules for EMU.
But diplomats admit that the fact the summit is being held unusally on a Monday and Tuesday, when financial markets will be open, could create an unwanted diversion from the IGC issue.

"Because finance ministers will be in Amsterdam, and because markets will be open, EMU is an issue that won't be allowed to go away and (that) could create a difficulty," one said. Normally summits are held at the weekend.

Diplomats said that the leaders, aware of keen market interest in financial issues rather than the uninspiring IGC, would probably use an agreement on the stability pact and choosing a design for the new euro coin as a signal that they were committed to keeping EMU on track.
"They wouldn't be taken seriously if they let EMU hijack their agenda. But, if they put it up the agenda, everyone would smell a crisis," the diplomat said.
Another said the summit's priority was to finish the IGC talks to concentrate on other pressing issues, such as monetary union, during the rest of the year.

Diplomats said EU finance ministers, meeting in Luxembourg next Sunday and Monday to discuss outstanding EMU issues including the pact and the post-EMU exchange rate mechanism, would probably try to head off any EMU problems before Amsterdam.
One diplomat joked that once EU leaders had chosen a new euro coin, they could at least toss it to see whether or not to go ahead with the project.
